triples.relationship: prophetic messages dated in Darius's second year
triples.rationale: Zechariah dates the Lord's word to the eighth month of Darius's second year. Haggai likewise dates a prophetic word to that king's second year, in the sixth month. The shared regnal year places the two messages in the same dated setting while preserving the different months.

triples.relationship: divine anger after the ancestors reject prophetic messages
triples.rationale: Zechariah recalls the Lord's great anger with the fathers before warning against their example. Chronicles describes the people mocking His prophets until His anger rose without healing, giving a particular account of the rejection and anger recalled by that warning.
triples.source_text: “The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger.

target_units.text: The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

triples.relationship: shared call to return with a promise of divine return
triples.rationale: Both passages command the people to return to the Lord and promise that He will return to them. Malachi places the same invitation after charges concerning the fathers' injustices and abandoned ordinances.
triples.source_text: You shall say to them: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Return to Me, and I will return to you, says the Lord.

target_units.text: from the injustices of your fathers. You have turned aside from My ordinances and have not guarded them. Return to Me, and I will return to you,” says the Lord Almighty. And you said, “How shall we return?”

triples.relationship: refusal to listen to the former prophets
triples.rationale: Zechariah warns against ancestors who ignored the former prophets' calls to turn from evil. Chronicles likewise describes God's repeated prophetic messages being mocked and His words treated as nothing.
triples.source_text: Do not become like your fathers, against whom the former prophets brought charges, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn away from your evil ways and your evil practices.’ But they did not listen attentively to Me, says the Lord.

target_units.text: The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

triples.relationship: human mortality contrasted with the continuing divine word
triples.rationale: Zechariah asks where the fathers are and whether the prophets live forever, before turning to God's words in the next unit. Isaiah similarly pictures mortal flesh as withering grass while God's word remains forever. The connection preserves the distinction between mortal messengers and their message.
triples.source_text: Your fathers—where are they? And the prophets—surely they will not live forever?

target_units.text: A voice says, “Cry out!” And I said, “What shall I cry?” All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass.
The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen;
but the word of our God remains for ever.

triples.relationship: prophetic words associated with realized judgment
triples.rationale: Zechariah calls for receiving God's words and ordinances given through the prophets and records acknowledgment that the Lord acted according to the people's ways. Chronicles describes deportation and desolation as fulfilling the Lord's word through Jeremiah. Both connect the people's experience of judgment with the prophetic word.
triples.source_text: Yet receive My words and My ordinances, all that I, in My Spirit, command My servants the prophets, who overtook your fathers.” And they answered and said, “As the Lord Almighty has arrayed Himself to act according to your ways and practices, so He acted toward you.”

target_units.text: He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,
to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.

triples.relationship: same-book sequence of dated prophetic revelations
triples.rationale: The opening message is dated to the eighth month of Darius's second year; this vision sequence begins on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the same year. The repeated prophet identification and regnal year establish the book's dated progression.

triples.relationship: same-book visions of colored horses between mountains
triples.rationale: The first vision places a mounted man and colored horses between shaded mountains. Chapter 6 presents chariots with colored horses emerging between bronze mountains. The repeated horses-and-mountains scene links the visions, while their colors, vehicles and mountain descriptions remain distinct.
triples.source_text: I saw in the night: look, a man mounted on a flame-red horse! He stood between the two shaded mountains, and behind him were flame-red, gray, dappled and white horses.

target_units.text: I turned and lifted my eyes and saw: look, four chariots coming out from between two mountains! The mountains were bronze mountains.
The first chariot had flame-red horses, and the second chariot black horses,
the third chariot white horses, and the fourth chariot dappled, gray horses.

triples.relationship: same-book request for interpretation of the horse visions
triples.rationale: In both visions Zechariah asks the angel what the presented figures are. Chapter 1 promises an explanation, while chapter 6 supplies one concerning the four winds. The repeated question connects the prophetic vision-and-interpretation pattern without equating all its figures.
triples.source_text: I said, “What are these, lord?” The angel speaking within me said to me, “I will show you what these are.”

target_units.text: I answered and said to the angel speaking within me, “What are these, lord?”
The angel speaking within me answered, “These are the four winds of heaven; they go out to stand beside the Lord of all the earth.

triples.relationship: same-book commission to travel around the earth
triples.rationale: The man explains that the Lord sent these figures to travel around the earth. In chapter 6 the gray horses seek to travel around the earth, receive the command to do so, and carry it out. Both vision scenes expressly describe this commission.
triples.source_text: The man standing between the mountains answered and said to me, “These are the ones the Lord has sent out to travel around the earth.”

target_units.text: and the gray ones were going out and looking to go and travel around the earth.” He said, “Go and travel around the earth!” And they traveled around the earth.

triples.relationship: same-book completion of a journey around the earth
triples.rationale: The first vision's travelers report that they have traveled around all the earth and found it quiet. Chapter 6 likewise reports the commanded travelers going around the earth. The shared completed journey connects the scenes; the report of quiet belongs to chapter 1.
triples.source_text: They answered the angel of the Lord standing between the mountains, “We have traveled around all the earth, and look, all the earth is inhabited and quiet.”

target_units.text: and the gray ones were going out and looking to go and travel around the earth.” He said, “Go and travel around the earth!” And they traveled around the earth.

triples.relationship: seventy years followed by an appeal or promise of restoration
triples.rationale: The angel asks about mercy for Jerusalem and Judah's cities in the seventieth year. Jeremiah promises a divine visitation and return when seventy years for Babylon approach fulfillment. The stated duration and renewed concern for the displaced people connect the passages.
triples.source_text: The angel of the Lord answered, “Lord Almighty, how long wilt Thou refuse mercy to Jerusalem and Judah’s cities, which Thou hast overlooked this seventieth year?”

target_units.text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.

triples.relationship: comfort concerning Jerusalem after her distress
triples.rationale: The Lord answers the angel's appeal for Jerusalem with good and comforting words. Isaiah likewise commands comforting God's people and speaking to Jerusalem's heart after her humiliation. Both introduce restoration with an explicit message of comfort.
triples.source_text: The Lord Almighty answered the angel speaking within me with good words and comforting speeches.

target_units.text: Comfort, comfort My people, says God.
You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

triples.relationship: same-book repeated declaration of jealousy for Jerusalem and Zion
triples.rationale: Both declarations name Jerusalem and Zion and describe the Lord's great jealousy for her. Chapter 8 repeats the earlier assurance while adding great wrath, preserving the book's stated divine concern for the city.
triples.source_text: The angel speaking within me said to me, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy,

target_units.text: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy; with great wrath I have been jealous for her.

triples.relationship: nations blamed for worsening the judgment of God's people
triples.rationale: Zechariah distinguishes the Lord's limited anger from the nations' participation in attacks that brought evils. Isaiah similarly says that God gave His inheritance into the Chaldean power's hand, yet condemns its lack of mercy and excessive burden on the elderly.
triples.source_text: and I am angry with great anger at the nations joining in assault, because I was a little angry, but they joined in attacking to bring evils.

target_units.text: “Sit stricken and enter darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans. You will certainly no longer be called a kingdom’s strength.
I was provoked against My people; you defiled My inheritance. I gave it into your hand, but you gave them no mercy; you made the elder’s yoke exceedingly heavy.

triples.relationship: the Lord's house in Jerusalem promised and then reported rebuilt
triples.rationale: Zechariah announces the rebuilding of the Lord's house in Jerusalem. Ezra reports the house rebuilt under prophetic encouragement and completed in Darius's sixth year. The link concerns the expressly named rebuilding, without treating the two dated statements as simultaneous.
triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and My house will be rebuilt in her, says the Lord Almighty, and a measure will again be extended over Jerusalem.”

target_units.text: The elders of the Jews and the Levites were building through the prophecy of Haggai the prophet and Zacharias son of Addo. They rebuilt and put it in order by the decree of the God of Israel and by the decree of Cyrus, Darius and Arthasastha, kings of the Persians.
They completed this house by the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.

triples.relationship: same-book renewed favor expressed through Jerusalem's inhabitation
triples.rationale: The Lord promises renewed good for the cities and renewed mercy and choice of Jerusalem. Chapter 8 describes His return to Jerusalem and elderly people and children again occupying her squares, making the promised renewed favor concrete.
triples.source_text: The angel speaking within me said to me, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Cities will again overflow with good things; the Lord will again have mercy on Zion and again choose Jerusalem.”

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: I will return to Zion and dwell within Jerusalem. Jerusalem will be called the True City, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty a Holy Mountain.
Thus says the Lord Almighty: Old men and old women will again sit in Jerusalem’s squares, each holding a staff in hand because of many days.
The city’s squares will be filled with boys and girls playing in her squares.

triples.relationship: horns interpreted as political powers in prophetic visions
triples.rationale: Zechariah sees four horns, identified in the following unit with powers that scattered Judah and Israel. Daniel interprets ten horns as ten kings. Both visions use horns for political powers, while the numbers and identified actions differ.
triples.source_text: I lifted my eyes and saw: look, four horns!

target_units.text: As for the kingdom’s ten horns, ten kings will arise, and another king will arise after them. He will surpass the earlier ones in evils and humble three kings.

triples.relationship: same-chapter explanation of the horns' scattering of Judah and Israel
triples.rationale: The angel first identifies the horns as those that scattered Judah and Israel. The later explanation repeats their scattering of Judah and shattering of Israel and describes nations lifting a horn against the Lord's land. The repeated charge gives the vision its stated national setting.
triples.source_text: I said to the angel speaking within me, “What are these, lord?” He said to me, “These are the horns that scattered Judah and Israel.”

target_units.text: I said, “What are these coming to do?” He said to me, “These horns that scattered Judah also shattered Israel, and none of them lifted a head. These entered to sharpen them for their hands—the four horns, the nations lifting a horn against the Lord’s land to scatter it.”

triples.relationship: visionary surveyor carrying measuring equipment
triples.rationale: Zechariah sees a man with a land-measuring cord before the explanation that he will measure Jerusalem. Ezekiel likewise sees a man carrying a builders' cord and measuring reed within a vision of a city-like structure and its enclosure. Both present a surveyor with explicit measuring equipment.
triples.source_text: I lifted my eyes and saw: look, a man with a land-measuring cord in his hand!

target_units.text: in a vision of God into Israel’s land and set me upon a very high mountain. Upon it, opposite, was something like a city’s structure.
He brought me in there, and behold, a man whose appearance was like gleaming copper. In his hand were a builders’ cord and a measuring reed, and he stood at the gate.

The man said to me, ‘Have you seen, son of man? See with your eyes, hear with your ears and set in your heart everything I show you, for you have entered here so that it might be shown to you. You will show Israel’s house everything you see.’

Behold, an enclosure surrounded the house outside. In the man’s hand was a reed measuring six cubits by the cubit and handbreadth. He measured the outer wall: its width equaled the reed, and its height equaled the reed.

triples.relationship: same-book promised measuring of Jerusalem enacted in a vision
triples.rationale: The earlier promise says a measure will again extend over Jerusalem. The man now states that he is going to measure Jerusalem's width and length. The shared city and measuring action connect promise and visionary scene.
triples.source_text: I said to him, “Where are you going?” He said to me, “To measure Jerusalem, to see how wide it is and how long.”

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and My house will be rebuilt in her, says the Lord Almighty, and a measure will again be extended over Jerusalem.”

triples.relationship: restored inhabitation with multiplied people and animals
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises Jerusalem's fruitful inhabitation because of many people and animals. Ezekiel likewise promises inhabited cities and multiplied humans and livestock upon Israel's mountains. Both explicitly combine restored settlement with human and animal abundance.
triples.source_text: and said to him, “Run and speak to that young man: Jerusalem will be inhabited fruitfully because of the multitude of people and animals within her.

target_units.text: I will multiply people upon you, all Israel’s house completely. The cities will be inhabited and the devastated land rebuilt.
I will multiply humans and livestock upon you, settle you as at your beginning and do you good as in your former times. You will know that I am the Lord.

triples.relationship: divine protection of Zion pictured with fire and glory
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises that the Lord will be Jerusalem's surrounding wall of fire and glory within her. Isaiah describes cloud, the light of burning fire and glory over Zion, followed by shelter from harsh conditions. Both join fire and glory with protection, using different protective images.
triples.source_text: I will be a wall of fire around her, says the Lord, and I will be glory within her.”

target_units.text: He will come, and it will be: a cloud will shade every place of Mount Zion and everything around her by day, and as of smoke and as of a light of fire burning by night; with all the glory it will be covered.
It will be shade from heat, shelter and concealment from harshness and rain.

triples.relationship: the Lord surrounding His people in Jerusalem's setting
triples.rationale: The Lord promises to surround Jerusalem as a wall of fire. The psalm compares the mountains around Jerusalem with the Lord around His people. Both portray His surrounding protection, without making the psalm's mountains a literal fiery wall.
triples.source_text: I will be a wall of fire around her, says the Lord, and I will be glory within her.”

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. Those trusting in the Lord are like Mount Zion; the one dwelling in Jerusalem will never be shaken.
Mountains are around her, and the Lord is around His people, from now and for ever.

triples.relationship: divine gathering from the reaches of dispersion
triples.rationale: Zechariah joins the call to flee the northern land with God's promise to gather from the four winds of heaven. Deuteronomy promises gathering from the nations and even from one end of heaven to the other. Both describe divine recovery from extensive dispersion.

target_units.text: then the Lord shall heal your sins, and have mercy upon you, and shall gather you again from all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you.
If your dispersion is from one end of heaven unto the other end of heaven, from thence shall the Lord your God gather you, and from thence shall the Lord your God take you.
And the Lord your God shall bring you into the land which your fathers inherited, and you shall inherit it; and He shall do you good, and make you more numerous than your fathers.

triples.relationship: explicit command to leave Babylon
triples.rationale: Zechariah commands those dwelling in daughter Babylon to escape safely to Zion. Isaiah likewise commands leaving Babylon and fleeing the Chaldeans while announcing the Lord's rescue of Jacob. The named place and commanded departure connect the passages.
triples.source_text: Escape safely to Zion, you who dwell in daughter Babylon!

triples.relationship: God's people compared with the vulnerable pupil of an eye
triples.rationale: Zechariah says touching the plundered people is like touching an eye's pupil. Deuteronomy describes the Lord guarding His people Jacob as an eye's pupil. Both use that particular bodily image to express the people's protected importance.

He sustained him in a wilderness land, in the thirst of burning heat, in a waterless place; He compassed him about, and instructed him, and kept him as the pupil of an eye.

triples.rationale: Zechariah warns the nations that touching the people is like touching an eye's pupil. The psalm asks God to guard the speaker as an eye's pupil amid surrounding enemies. Both connect the vulnerable eye image with protection from hostility.
triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord Almighty: “After glory He has sent me against the nations that plundered you, for whoever touches you is like one touching the pupil of his eye.

Guard me as the pupil of an eye; in the shelter of Thy wings Thou wilt shelter me,
from the ungodly who made me miserable. My enemies surrounded my soul.

triples.relationship: reversal of the relation between captors and servants
triples.rationale: Zechariah announces that the plundering nations will become spoils for those serving them. Isaiah likewise says former captors will become captives and former rulers will be ruled, followed by rest from harsh slavery. Both expressly reverse domination.

triples.rationale: Zechariah calls daughter Zion to delight and rejoice because the Lord will come and dwell within her. Zephaniah similarly calls Zion and Jerusalem to rejoice and names the saving Lord within her. The address, joy and divine presence closely correspond.
triples.source_text: “Delight and rejoice, daughter Zion, for look, I am coming and will dwell within you,” says the Lord.

The Lord removed your wrongdoings and has redeemed you from your enemies’ hand. The Lord, King of Israel, is within you; you will see evils no more.
At that time the Lord will say to Jerusalem, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands hang loose.
The Lord your God is within you; mighty, He shall save you. He shall bring gladness upon you, and renew you in His love; and He shall rejoice over you with delight, as on a day of feasting.”

triples.rationale: Zechariah promises that many nations will take refuge with the Lord and become His people. Isaiah welcomes foreigners attached to the Lord into His holy mountain and house of prayer for all nations. Both place people from other nations within the Lord's gathered community.

said the Lord who gathers Israel’s scattered people, “for I will gather a gathering to him.”

triples.relationship: the Lord's people described as His portion and inheritance
triples.rationale: Zechariah calls Judah the Lord's portion on the holy land. Deuteronomy likewise calls Jacob His portion and Israel the measured lot of His inheritance. The comparison concerns that stated belonging, while preserving each passage's named people.
triples.source_text: The Lord will inherit Judah as His portion on the holy land and again choose Jerusalem.

target_units.text: And His people Jacob became the portion of the Lord; Israel, the measured lot of His inheritance.

triples.relationship: universal reverence before the Lord in His holy dwelling
triples.rationale: Zechariah calls all flesh to reverence because the Lord has risen from His holy clouds. Habakkuk calls all the earth to revere Him in His holy sanctuary. Both combine a universal summons to reverence with His holy dwelling, described differently.
triples.source_text: Let all flesh be reverent before the Lord, for He has risen from His holy clouds.

target_units.text: But the Lord is in His holy sanctuary; let all the earth revere Him.”

triples.relationship: a slanderer positioned at the accused person's right hand
triples.rationale: Joshua stands before the Lord's angel with the slanderer at his right hand to oppose him. The psalm likewise pictures a slanderer standing at someone's right hand in a context of judgment. The position and accusatory role connect the scenes.
triples.source_text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, with the slanderer standing at his right hand to oppose him.

When he is judged, may he come out condemned, and let his prayer become sin.

triples.rationale: Zechariah's vision places the slanderer beside Joshua to oppose him before the Lord's angel. Both feature an adversary bringing a challenge concerning a named servant, without equating the servants or proceedings.
triples.source_text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, with the slanderer standing at his right hand to oppose him.

The Lord said to the devil, “Where have you come from?” The devil answered the Lord, “I have come after going around the earth and walking through the world beneath heaven.”
The Lord said to him, “Have you paid attention in your mind to My servant Job? For among those on earth there is no man like him—blameless, true, God-fearing, keeping away from every evil deed.”
The devil answered before the Lord, “Does Job worship God for nothing?

Hast Thou not fenced in what is outside him and what is inside his house, and everything around all that belongs to him? Thou hast blessed the works of his hands and made his livestock numerous in the land.
But stretch out Thy hand and touch everything he has; surely he will curse Thee to Thy face.”

triples.relationship: shared appeal for the Lord to rebuke an adversary
triples.rationale: Zechariah addresses the slanderer with the words 'May the Lord rebuke you.' Jude reports Michael using the same appeal while disputing with the devil concerning Moses' body. The verbal correspondence is explicit, while the occasions differ.
triples.source_text: The Lord said to the slanderer, “May the Lord rebuke you, slanderer! May the Lord, who chose Jerusalem, rebuke you! Look, is this not like a brand pulled from fire?”

target_units.text: But Michael the archangel, when he was contending with the devil and disputing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said, “May the Lord rebuke you.”

triples.relationship: shared image of a brand pulled from fire
triples.rationale: The question concerning Joshua likens him to a brand pulled from fire. Amos likewise describes the people as a firebrand snatched from fire after an overthrow. Both use the particular rescue image, with different persons and settings.
triples.source_text: The Lord said to the slanderer, “May the Lord rebuke you, slanderer! May the Lord, who chose Jerusalem, rebuke you! Look, is this not like a brand pulled from fire?”

target_units.text: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched from fire. Yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

triples.relationship: unclean clothing associated with lawlessness
triples.rationale: Joshua's filthy garments are interpreted in the next unit through the removal of his lawless deeds. Isaiah likewise links the people's uncleanness and rag-like righteousness with their lawless deeds. triples.source_text: Joshua was clothed in filthy garments and standing before the angel.

triples.relationship: new clothing expressing divine restoration
triples.rationale: Joshua's filthy garments are removed as his lawless deeds are taken away, and he is clothed in a full-length robe. Isaiah's speaker likewise rejoices in being clothed by the Lord with salvation and joy. Both associate new clothing with divine restoration, while naming the garments differently.
triples.source_text: He answered and said to those standing before him, “Remove the filthy garments from him.” He said to him, “Look, I have taken away your lawless deeds; clothe him in a robe reaching to the feet,

triples.rationale: Joshua receives clean headwear and garments in his role as high priest. Exodus prescribes holy priestly garments for Aaron, including a full-length robe and turban. The shared priestly dress connects the scenes; Zechariah adds cleansing within the vision.
triples.source_text: and put a clean turban on his head.” They clothed him in garments and put a clean turban on his head, while the angel of the Lord stood by.

You shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honour and glory.
Speak to everyone skilled in understanding whom I have filled with a spirit of perception. They shall make Aaron’s holy robe for the sanctuary, in which he shall serve Me as priest.

These are the robes they shall make: a breastpiece, a shoulder-piece, a full-length robe, a tasselled tunic, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy robes for Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.

triples.rationale: Joshua is charged to keep the Lord's commands and guard His court as he governs His house. Numbers likewise assigns priestly and Levitical service to keeping the charges and furnishings of the Tent. Both connect religious office with responsibility for the sanctuary.
triples.source_text: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in My ways and keep My commands, you will govern My house. If you also guard My court, I will give you those who move about among these standing here.

target_units.text: Take the tribe of Levi, and you shall set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall minister unto him;
And they shall keep his charges and the charges of the sons of Israel before the Tent of Testimony, performing the work of the Tent.
And they shall keep all the furnishings of the Tent of Testimony and the charges of the sons of Israel, according to all the work of the Tent.

triples.relationship: same-book recurrence of the promised figure named Rising
triples.rationale: The Lord promises to bring His servant Rising before Joshua and his companions. Chapter 6 again announces a man named Rising and says he will build the Lord's house. The repeated name connects the two announcements.
triples.source_text: Listen now, Joshua the high priest, you and your neighbors sitting before you, for they are men who watch for portents. Look, I am bringing My servant, Rising.

triples.rationale: Zechariah commands asking the Lord for seasonal rain and says He gives winter rain and vegetation. Jeremiah likewise asks whether idols can bring rain and looks to the Lord as maker of these things. Both locate the sought rainfall in His agency.
triples.source_text: Ask the Lord for rain in its season, early and late. The Lord made appearances and will give them winter rain, to each person vegetation in the field.

target_units.text: Is there among the nations’ idols one who brings rain? Can heaven give its fullness? Is it not Thou Thyself? And we will wait for Thee, because Thou madest all these things.

triples.relationship: false visions and empty assurances mislead the people
triples.rationale: Zechariah condemns diviners' false visions, false dreams and vain comfort before describing the people's distress. Ezekiel likewise condemns false visions and vain divinations that mislead the people with declarations of peace when none exists. Both expose deceptive religious reassurance.
triples.source_text: For those making pronouncements spoke troubles, the diviners false visions; they were telling false dreams and giving vain comfort. Therefore they were carried away like sheep and mistreated, because there was no healing.

target_units.text: They see false things and divine vain things, those who say, ‘The Lord says,’ although the Lord has not sent them; and they began to establish a word.
Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations?
Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations vain, therefore behold, I am against you, says the Lord,

and I will stretch out My hand against the prophets who see false things and utter vain things. They will not belong to My people’s instruction, nor be written in the register of the house of Israel, nor enter Israel’s land. They will know that I am the Lord.
Because they misled My people, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace, and this one builds a wall, and they coat it—if it is going to fall,

triples.relationship: judgment of shepherds joined to renewed care for the flock
triples.rationale: Zechariah announces wrath against shepherds and the Lord's attention to His flock, Judah's house. Jeremiah likewise condemns shepherds who scatter the sheep and promises gathering and renewed shepherding. Both contrast failed leadership with divine care for the people.
triples.source_text: My wrath was provoked against the shepherds, and I will attend to the lambs. The Lord God Almighty will attend to His flock, Judah’s house, and make them like His splendid horse in battle.

target_units.text: O shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of My pasture!
Therefore thus says the Lord to those shepherding My people: You scattered My sheep and drove them out without visiting them. Behold, I am exacting justice from you according to your evil practices.
And I will receive the remnant of My people from all the land where I drove them out, and establish them in their pasture; they will increase and multiply.
And I will raise shepherds for them who will tend them, and they will no longer fear or be frightened, says the Lord.

triples.relationship: confidence in the Lord contrasted with defeated horse power
triples.rationale: Zechariah's fighters prevail because the Lord is with them, while horse riders are shamed. The psalm likewise contrasts reliance on chariots and horses with magnification in the Lord's name and describes the opponents falling. Both make the Lord, rather than cavalry, decisive.
triples.source_text: They will be like fighters trampling mud in the roads in battle; they will draw up for combat because the Lord is with them, and horse riders will be put to shame.

target_units.text: These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

triples.relationship: Judah and Joseph included together in divine restoration
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises strength for Judah and salvation for Joseph, followed by settlement and renewed relation to their God. Ezekiel likewise brings Joseph and Judah together, gathers Israel into the land and promises that they will be His people and He their God. Both explicitly include these named houses in restoration.
triples.source_text: I will strengthen Judah’s house and save Joseph’s house. I will settle them because I have loved them; they will be as though I had not turned them away, for I am the Lord their God and will listen to them.

target_units.text: say to them, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take Joseph’s tribe through Ephraim’s hand, and Israel’s tribes attached to him, and place them upon Judah’s tribe. They will become one staff in Judah’s hand.
The staffs upon which you wrote will be in your hand before them,

and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

so that they no longer defile themselves with their idols. I will deliver them from all their lawless deeds in which they sinned and cleanse them. They will be My people, and I, the Lord, will be their God.

triples.relationship: Judah and Israel gathered within restored belonging to God
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises restoring Judah and Joseph as though not rejected. Hosea likewise reverses the declaration 'not My people' and announces Judah and Israel gathering together. Both combine the named people's restoration with reversal of alienation, using their respective house names.
triples.source_text: I will strengthen Judah’s house and save Joseph’s house. I will settle them because I have loved them; they will be as though I had not turned them away, for I am the Lord their God and will listen to them.

target_units.text: The number of Israel’s sons was like the sand of the sea, which will not be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.
Judah’s sons and Israel’s sons will gather together, appoint one authority for themselves and come up from the land, for great is Jezreel’s day.
Say to your brother, ‘My People,’ and to your sister, ‘Shown Mercy.’

triples.relationship: wine used to describe a gladdened human heart
triples.rationale: Zechariah compares Ephraim's rejoicing heart with the effect of wine. The psalm directly says wine gladdens the human heart. The particular wine-and-heart association explains the comparison, without turning Zechariah's promised joy into a command to drink.
triples.source_text: They will be like Ephraim’s fighters, and their heart will rejoice as with wine. Their children will see and be glad; their heart will rejoice in the Lord.

target_units.text: and wine gladdens the human heart, to brighten the face with oil, and bread makes the human heart firm.

triples.relationship: a divine signal followed by gathering the scattered people
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises the Lord's signal and reception of the redeemed people. Isaiah likewise describes His raised signal and gathering of Israel's lost and Judah's scattered ones. Both expressly connect signaling with gathering.
triples.source_text: I will signal to them and receive them, for I will redeem them; they will multiply as they were once many.

target_units.text: He will raise a signal to the nations and gather Israel’s lost ones; He will gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings.

triples.relationship: remembrance and return while dispersed among peoples
triples.rationale: Zechariah describes those sown among peoples remembering God from far away and returning with their children. Deuteronomy likewise speaks of taking the Lord's words to heart among the nations of dispersion, returning to Him and being gathered. Both place inward recollection and return within exile.
triples.source_text: I will sow them among peoples, and those far away will remember Me; they will nourish their children and return.

target_units.text: And it shall be, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse which I have set before your face, and you receive them into your heart among all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you,
and you return unto the Lord your God, and obey His voice according to all that I command you this day, with all your heart and with all your soul,
then the Lord shall heal your sins, and have mercy upon you, and shall gather you again from all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you.

triples.relationship: recovery of the remnant from Egypt and the Assyrians
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises bringing the people back from Egypt and receiving them from the Assyrians. Isaiah likewise names the Assyrians and Egypt among the places from which the remaining people are recovered and gathered. The named regions provide the particular connection.
triples.source_text: I will bring them back from Egypt’s land and receive them from the Assyrians. I will bring them into Gilead and Lebanon, and not even one of them will be left behind.

target_units.text: On that day the Lord will again show His hand, to be zealous for the remaining remnant of the people left from the Assyrians, Egypt, Babylonia, Ethiopia, the Elamites, the sun’s rising and Arabia.
He will raise a signal to the nations and gather Israel’s lost ones; He will gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings.

triples.relationship: waters made passable in the people's return
triples.rationale: Zechariah describes passage through a narrow sea, struck waves and dried river depths while foreign domination is removed. Isaiah likewise describes Egypt's sea laid waste and a river struck so that the remnant can pass through in sandals. Both join altered waters with return, preserving their distinct geography and actions.
triples.source_text: They will pass through a narrow sea and strike waves in the sea; all the rivers’ depths will dry up. All the Assyrians’ arrogance will be removed, and Egypt’s scepter will be taken away.

target_units.text: The Lord will lay Egypt’s sea waste and bring His hand upon the river with a violent wind. He will strike seven ravines so that one may pass through it in sandals.
There will be a passage for My remaining people in Egypt, and it will be for Israel as on the day it came out of Egypt’s land.

triples.relationship: strength and exaltation associated with the Lord's name
triples.rationale: Zechariah promises strength in the Lord and boasting in His name. The psalm likewise describes His saving strength and says the people will be magnified in the Lord their God's name. Both place the people's confidence in Him rather than their own resources.
triples.source_text: I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and they will boast in His name, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Now I know that the Lord saved His anointed; He will hear him from His holy heaven; in mighty acts is the salvation of His right hand.
These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

triples.relationship: Lebanon and cedars consumed in announced judgment
triples.rationale: Zechariah calls Lebanon to open its doors for fire to devour its cedars. Jeremiah likewise addresses Judah's royal house with Lebanon imagery and announces its chosen cedars cut down and thrown into fire. The shared Lebanon, cedar and fire imagery is explicit, with different addressed settings.
triples.source_text: Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars!

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord against the house of Judah’s king: You are Gilead to Me, the head of Lebanon; surely I will make you a wilderness, cities that will not be inhabited.
And I will bring against you a destroying man and his axe, and they will cut down your chosen cedars and cast them into the fire.

triples.relationship: the fall of Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks
triples.rationale: Zechariah calls for lament over the fallen cedar and devastated Bashan oaks. Isaiah likewise includes the high cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan among those reached by the Lord's humbling day. The two named kinds and places connect the imagery.
triples.source_text: Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have suffered greatly! Wail, Bashan’s oaks, for the thick-grown forest has been torn down!

target_units.text: For the Lord Sabaoth has a day against every insolent and arrogant person, against everyone high and elevated; they will be humbled,
against every cedar of Lebanon among the high and elevated, and against every oak tree of Bashan,

triples.relationship: shepherds lament the destruction of their greatness and pasture
triples.rationale: Zechariah reports shepherds lamenting their afflicted greatness alongside roaring lions. Jeremiah likewise commands shepherds to mourn and reports their cries because the Lord destroyed their grazing places. The shared shepherd-lament scene is particular, without equating every accompanying image.
triples.source_text: A sound of shepherds lamenting, for their greatness has suffered! A sound of lions roaring, for the Jordan’s proud swelling has suffered!

target_units.text: Raise a shout, shepherds, and cry out; beat yourselves in mourning, rams of the sheep, because your days for slaughter have been fulfilled, and you will fall like choice rams.
And flight will perish from the shepherds, and salvation from the rams of the sheep.
A sound of shepherds crying and of sheep and rams shouting, because the Lord destroyed their grazing places,

triples.relationship: a flock marked for slaughter
triples.rationale: Zechariah commands shepherding sheep destined for slaughter. Jeremiah likewise addresses shepherds and rams as their days for slaughter arrive and escape fails. Both present a doomed flock, though one begins a symbolic shepherding action and the other commands mourning.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: “Shepherd the sheep destined for slaughter,

target_units.text: Raise a shout, shepherds, and cry out; beat yourselves in mourning, rams of the sheep, because your days for slaughter have been fulfilled, and you will fall like choice rams.
And flight will perish from the shepherds, and salvation from the rams of the sheep.

triples.relationship: shepherds profit from a flock they fail to care for
triples.rationale: Zechariah describes buyers slaughtering sheep, sellers rejoicing in wealth and shepherds feeling nothing for them. Ezekiel likewise condemns shepherds who consume the flock's products and slaughter fattened animals without feeding or healing the sheep. Both indict exploitation joined to failed care.
triples.source_text: which their buyers were slaughtering without regret; their sellers said, ‘Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich!’ Their shepherds felt nothing for them.

target_units.text: “Son of man, prophesy against Israel’s shepherds. Prophesy and say to the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, surely shepherds do not feed themselves? Do shepherds not feed the sheep?
Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fattened animal, but you do not feed My sheep.
You have not strengthened the weak, restored the sick to health, bound up the broken, brought back the wandering or sought the lost. You have worn down the strong with toil.

triples.relationship: same-book people handed over against their neighbors
triples.rationale: Zechariah 11 announces each person being handed into a neighbor's and a king's hands as the land is cut apart. Chapter 8 likewise describes a period when God sends everyone against his neighbor and travel has no peace. The mutual hostility within the land links the judgments.
triples.source_text: Therefore I will no longer spare the land’s residents, says the Lord. Look, I am handing over human beings, each into his neighbor’s hands and his king’s hands. They will cut the land to pieces, and I will certainly not rescue from their hand.”

target_units.text: Before those days people’s wages will bring no benefit, and animals’ hire will not exist; those going out or coming in will have no peace because of affliction. I will send everyone out against his neighbor.

triples.relationship: same-chapter two named staffs enacted as symbols of broken relations
triples.rationale: The shepherd takes the staffs Beauty and Measuring Cord. The later actions discard the beautiful staff to dissolve a covenant and the second staff to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel. The named objects explicitly connect their introduction with their subsequent symbolic actions.
triples.source_text: I will shepherd the sheep destined for slaughter into Canaan’s land. I will take two staffs for myself—I called one Beauty and the other Measuring Cord—and I will shepherd the sheep.

target_units.text: I will take my beautiful staff and throw it away, to dissolve my covenant that I made with all the peoples.
It will be dissolved on that day, and the Canaanites—the sheep being guarded—will know that it is the Lord’s word.
I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

The Lord said to me, “Put them into the smelting furnace and examine whether it is approved, as I was tested on their behalf.” I took the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the Lord’s house, into the smelting furnace.
I threw away the second staff, Measuring Cord, to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel.

triples.relationship: neighbors consuming one another's flesh under judgment
triples.rationale: Zechariah announces refusal to shepherd and says the remaining people will devour their neighbors' flesh. Jeremiah likewise announces each eating his neighbor's flesh during siege, alongside the flesh of children. The severe image is shared, while siege is explicit in Jeremiah.
triples.source_text: I said, “I will not shepherd you. Let the dying die, and let the failing fail; let those remaining each devour his neighbor’s flesh.”

target_units.text: And they will eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and each will eat his neighbor’s flesh in the encirclement and siege with which their enemies will besiege them.

triples.relationship: a covenant relationship described as broken
triples.rationale: Zechariah's discarded staff symbolizes dissolution of a covenant made with all the peoples. Jeremiah contrasts the promised new covenant with the fathers' failure to remain in the earlier covenant and God's disregard of them. Both describe the breakdown of a covenant relation, while the parties and symbolic action remain distinct.
triples.source_text: I will take my beautiful staff and throw it away, to dissolve my covenant that I made with all the peoples.

target_units.text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,

not according to the covenant I made with their fathers on the day I took their hand to bring them out of Egypt’s land, because they did not remain in My covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

triples.relationship: thirty silver pieces weighed out as a payment
triples.rationale: Zechariah's shepherd receives wages weighed out as thirty silver pieces. Matthew likewise reports thirty silver coins weighed out to Judas when he offers to hand Jesus over. The precise amount and weighed payment connect the passages, without identifying wages and betrayal as the same transaction.
triples.source_text: I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

target_units.text: Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
and said, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand Him over to you?” They weighed out for him thirty silver coins.
From then on he sought a suitable opportunity to hand Him over.

triples.relationship: a specified payment of thirty in silver
triples.rationale: Zechariah names thirty silver pieces as the shepherd's wages. Exodus specifies thirty didrachmas of silver paid to a slave's master when a bull gores the slave. Both give a thirty-unit silver payment, with their different units and legal or narrative functions preserved.
triples.source_text: I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

target_units.text: And if the bull gores a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty didrachmas of silver to their master, and the bull shall be stoned.

triples.relationship: thirty silver coins thrown into the sacred house with different dispositions
triples.rationale: Zechariah throws thirty silver pieces into the Lord's house, into a smelting furnace. Matthew reports Judas throwing the returned thirty coins into the sanctuary, after which priests buy the potter's field. The temple disposal and sum connect the accounts; furnace and potter's field remain different, and Matthew's quoted attribution to Jeremiah is preserved.
triples.source_text: The Lord said to me, “Put them into the smelting furnace and examine whether it is approved, as I was tested on their behalf.” I took the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the Lord’s house, into the smelting furnace.

saying, “I sinned by handing over innocent blood.” They said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”
He threw the silver coins into the sanctuary and withdrew; then he went away and hanged himself.
The chief priests took the silver coins and said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because they are the price of blood.”
After taking counsel, they bought the potter’s field with them as a burial place for strangers.
Therefore that field has been called Field of Blood until today.
Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty silver coins, the price of the One priced, whom some of the sons of Israel priced,
and gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

triples.relationship: contrasting staff actions concerning Judah and Israel
triples.rationale: Zechariah discards Measuring Cord to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel. Ezekiel instead joins staffs representing Judah and Joseph with Israel into one, explaining the end of their division. The symbolic staffs concern the relationship of the named peoples, but the actions and outcomes contrast.
triples.source_text: I threw away the second staff, Measuring Cord, to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel.

target_units.text: ‘Son of man, take a staff for yourself and write upon it Judah and Israel’s sons attached to him. Take a second staff for yourself and write upon it, For Joseph—Ephraim’s staff—and all Israel’s sons joined to him.
Join them to one another for yourself as one staff, binding them together, and they will be in your hand.
When your people’s sons say to you, Will you not tell us what these things mean to you?

say to them, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take Joseph’s tribe through Ephraim’s hand, and Israel’s tribes attached to him, and place them upon Judah’s tribe. They will become one staff in Judah’s hand.
The staffs upon which you wrote will be in your hand before them,

and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
